a good idea if it will help you get back to full Vitality. Finally, once you've gained the Breath of Life Skills, you can recover Vitality by landing Deathblows. There are two Breath of Life Skills in the game, each

allowing you to recover  $10\%$  Vitality per Deathblow. When stacked, they recover  $20\%$  of your Vitality. Please see the Shinobi Skills section for more detail on these.

# Guarding (LB/L1)

Guarding is performed by holding down  $\underline{\mathbb{L}}\mathbb{B} / \underline{\mathbb{L}}\mathbb{I}$ . It will nullify the Vitality damage of basic attacks, though as mentioned previously, not those with special properties. See the chart here for detailed information on how much Vitality damage is reduced by guarding. Guarding won't fully protect against Posture damage—though it will reduce it to a degree.

# > Guard Vitality Damage Reduction

![](images/e720f4471621724184aa2e5ad031a77c36f113807c91b2556b3ffba06829cc00.jpg)

Guarding only protects you from the front, not the back. When you are surrounded by enemies, it's often best to maneuver into a more favorable position, from which you can adequately defend yourself. However, the Loaded Umbrella tool will allow you to guard attacks from all directions.

Many attacks in Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice are executed very quickly and cannot be reasonably guarded just by reacting to them; they exist simply to test your guard. So, it's important to have your guard up when engaging the enemy—especially since it allows you to recover Posture much more quickly than normal. Guarding comes at the cost of mobility, however, as you can only walk while guarding. This means that when on the defensive, you're forced to make a tactical decision whether to hold your ground or try to

evade the incoming attack. Playing too passively and guarding too much will simply result in your Posture being broken—a balance needs to be struck between offense and defense.

# > Guard Crush

Certain powerful attacks from enemies will crush your guard, preventing you from guarding follow-up attacks and leaving you totally vulnerable to incoming attacks from surrounding enemies. Some bosses can follow up with highly damaging attacks, so it's crucial to avoid guarding against such moves—instead you should try to evade or deflect them.

Some Tools and Combat Arts, such as the Loaded Axe and Ichimonji, can also be used to crush your opponent's guard. If these

moves are guarded, the force of their impact leaves the opponent completely unable to retaliate and significantly weakens their Posture. Guard Crushing attacks can also often be used to interrupt an enemy's Armored Attacks, in addition to dealing more stun damage against Super Armored foes. You'll see this noted as a property in the Skills and Prosthetic Tools sections later in this guide.

# Brace Guard

If you are hit by certain heavy attacks you will enter a reeling stumble animation (see P.30 for more on this). A Brace Guard is unique defensive option you can adopt during a stumble that lets you recover a little faster. This effectively operates like a regular guard, letting you guard or deflect incoming attacks.

![](images/e526cdba03a45166cadb43a9091892bc34e8e2bea793bcd9886e61f700cfd6ee.jpg)

After being guard broken you are vulnerable to further attacks.

# Deflection

Deflection is a high-risk, high-reward technique that can either completely turn the tides of battle, or lead to a quick and untimely death if miscalculated. Instead of simply holding the button to guard, press it the moment before an attack connects, and you will swat it away with a deflect.

You don't necessarily have to tap the guard button in order to deflect; you can also press and hold it--any attack that comes your way during the animation where you raise your sword will be deflected. This means you can hold guard after any action, such as attack or step dodging, and if the next enemy attack connects while you are raising your sword to guard it will be deflected. This isn't something you can really plan for, but it reinforces the point to try and keep your guard up until you can assess a situation.

Successfully deflecting an attack deals Posture damage to an enemy. If your attacks are deflected by an enemy, however, you will receive no Posture damage. In many cases, deflecting also gives you the advantage and allows you to start pressuring the enemy with further attacks. By pressing R/R right after a deflect you will transition naturally in a counter-slash, which can then transition into your basic five hit attack combo. In this way, you can turn an enemy's offense against them, and use it to start initiating your own attacks. Enemies capable of deflecting will almost assuredly do so after guarding a few strikes. At that point its important to stop attacking and prepare to defend against their counter-attack.

Do note that deflecting an attack will still inflict damage to your Posture gauge, though it's significantly lower than guarding, which is already lower than being hit by the attack. Your Posture can also never be broken by a deflect, even if it is maxed out and flashing. Deflecting also reduces the Vitality damage you would have taken had you simply guarded against certain types of damage. Finally, deflecting will completely nullify Vitality damage from Piercing and Thrust attacks, as well as severely reducing Spirit and Fire.

![](images/2d5e5f4c512420fc415b08af073df41673a315ccd7e0d6d12ed9857a530ebd7d.jpg)

Deflecting causes bright yellow sparks to fly off your weapon.

![](images/e7ff2b6109bb93521161317597293260b48bff3ddce59acc9ffa369af4ca91df.jpg)

Remember that you can deflect projectiles too.

# > Deflect Vitality Damage Reduction

![](images/e33d07c2f893bf77ce58aa61d9c89218e949ca3aba188a431462d3fb930a7e00.jpg)

# >Deflection Advice

Deflection is a key, fundamental skill that will decide the outcome of many battles. Once mastered, nearly every enemy attack can be turned against them. Here's some general advice on mastering deflecting:

1. Many attacks begin very quickly, so it's important to have your guard up when engaging the enemy. If you feel confident you can deflect the attack, you can then quickly release guard and press it again—allowing you to deflect immediately out of a guard. This will add a layer of protective insurance to your deflects.  
2. Don't think of deflection as a reaction test, and don't try to deflect absolutely everything. Many of the enemy's attacks are simply too fast, and some intentionally wind up attacks in order to bait you into an ill-timed deflect. Instead, you should try to familiarize yourself with the timing of enemy attacks and strings before attempting any deflects. For example, many enemies can be provoked into a predictable attack after you hit them once. Others will always follow-up certain attacks after another in a pattern, which can be exploited to your advantage. Familiarity is key.  
3. Don't just repeatedly press the guard button in the vague hopes of deflecting an attack. The window for a deflect is roughly 1/5th of a second. This sounds small, but as long as you deflect with intentionality, it's actually quite generous. However, if you tap the guard button rapidly this window becomes more and more strict with each button press, going down on the fourth press to just 1/30th of a second. This greatly diminishes your probability of successfully deflecting an attack. Deflect with confidence and intentionality.

# >Deflect Stun

After deflecting an enemy attack, they will very often enter a stun animation. Against most enemies you can then either land a hit or attack their guard with a counter-slash. However, this is not always the case; deflecting certain moves will not result in a deflect stun, so retaliating immediately after may be risky. Consecutive Attacks are a good example of this.

# >Consecutive Attacks

Consecutive Attacks are multi-hitting attack strings that will keep on going whether you deflect them or not. Since these consist of many attacks back-to-back, all of which can be individually deflected, they present a good opportunity to inflict massive Posture damage on the enemy within a very short space of time. Especially since deflecting the Consecutive Attack all the way to its end will often yield a deflect stun on top of this, allowing you to counter-slash and attack the enemy for even more damage.

However, a move doesn't necessarily need to be part of a Consecutive Attack in order for it to be immune to a deflect stun. Such moves operate outside the norm, however, and will be pointed out within the relevant enemy's entry in the Opposing Forces chapter, starting on P.344.

![](images/5ed5dc950bb73188846d74f710c3404baaf118570dcef900bba3d0570bcd63c4.jpg)  
Against slower attacks, simply hold guard after attempting to deflect and you'll be safe either way.

# > Guard Locking Strings

Many Consecutive Attacks are also part of attack strings that lock you into guarding; if you guard the first attack in the string, you can actually let go of the guard button and you'll continue to guard the following attacks. This makes it easier to try to deflect, since even if you miss the timing you will still guard, so there is effectively no risk. All guard locking strings are considered Consecutive Attacks, but not all Consecutive Attacks will lock you into guarding. Guard locking mostly occurs against very fast-paced strings; when and where you can safely release guard during an attack so that you can attempt to deflect will be covered in the enemy strategies of the Opposing Forces chapter.

![](images/f6c261bf934ec46bcc9368482beff75dbc518562e9f5df508cefa49368933807.jpg)  
Lady Butterfly has many Consecutive Attacks...

![](images/738e69b0f099a8a8f6fec698a4da863ebbf22ca4596501ee236e2ddacd5bf166.jpg)  
...So deflecting well can drain her Posture quickly.

There are two elements to combat that you must unlock and equip in specific slots: Combat Arts and Ninjutsu. Here we'll explain how they fit into the overall combat puzzle; for much more detail on each Combat Art and Ninjutsu type, read through the Shinobi Skills section, starting on P.46.

# > Combat Arts

Combat Arts are special Skills that you'll find along the adventure that can be activated by pressing  $\underline{\mathbb{L}1 / \mathbb{L}8} +\underline{\mathbb{R}1 / \mathbb{R}8}$ . Each one offers you a new means for dealing with either groups of enemies or single targets, and will greatly increase your options during battle; some are purely offensive, while others also have defensive properties. Most do not cost Spirit Emblems, but some of the more powerful ones do, forcing you to balance their use with your Tools or risk running out mid fight. All of this means that each Combat Art's utility is potentially wildly different and must be judged on its own terms. You can only equip one at a time, though, so judging which one you'll need in a particular situation is something you'll need to do often, once you have a few unlocked—having the ideal one available for use can make some battles go much smoother.

# > Ninjutsu Techniques

Like Combat Arts, Ninjustu Techniques have their own slot, and you can only equip one at a time, but unlike Combat Arts, you can only acquire these techniques by defeating specific bosses rather than unlocking them in a skill tree. Activating one requires you to first land a Backstab Deathblow on a non-boss enemy that it would

# Swordplay

kill, and then you need to press the attack button again during the animation to trigger it. Ninjutsu Techniques are far fewer in number than Combat Arts, but their effects are extremely potent, and this is reflected in their relatively high Spirit Emblem cost. Initiating combat with a Backstab Deathblow on an enemy and then activating a Ninjutsu Technique is often the easiest way of using them, but if you have the Vault Over Skill, they become a powerful option that you can employ at any time during combat.

![](images/5f65a55d31c24079fca4a2c2986540fcf97901c1feaafdea24a46e566ff251e0.jpg)  
Ninjutsu are usually not worth using when there's only a single enemy in the area.

Swordplay is the umbrella term used to describe the interplaying systems of attacking, guarding, counter-slashing and deflecting. Put together, they replicate the back-and-forth clash of swords between skilled duelists. In Sekiro, this works beautifully, because the Swordplay system lets you get to know your opponent and their possible actions and reactions—enemies that guard or deflect your attacks can have a set of responses that they will only use at these times. It is through learning these responses that you can master combat.

Swordplay represents the battle between you and your opponent to choose the correct attacks and responses to deplete the other's Posture gauge. This battle lies at the heart of Sekiro's combat system, and it cannot be emphasized enough just how crucial it is to master. Swordplay is the reason why the Posture bars take front and center in the middle of the screen; they are the most important gauges to keep track of.

Remember that both deflecting and attacking will inflict Posture damage; attacks that hit or are guarded will deplete Posture. This means that, against every enemy that engages in Swordplay, no matter how threatening they may seem, getting close to them and using the correct sequence of attacking, counter-slashing and deflecting will be the optimal route to victory.

# > Swordplay Reactions

The four key interaction types used to trigger Swordplay Reactions are: guarding an enemy's attacks, deflecting an enemy's attacks, striking your opponent's guard, and lastly, causing your opponent to deflect. Some enemies will only react under one of those situations, while some more complex opponents may have a plethora of reactions tied to multiple categories. Although less frequent, it's also possible for a few opponents to react when struck with a direct hit.

To emphasize how Swordplay reactions work, we'll break down some possible actions and responses that General Naomori Kawarada (encountered in Ashina Outskirts) can use based on the defensive or offensive actions you take. Guarding this Samurai General's slashes will often cause him to aggressively attack with a flurry of quick overhead slashes that are designed to batter your guard until your Posture has been depleted. This is a unique reaction that will never happen unless you guard his slashes.

Attacks performed in response to your Swordplay actions can sometimes also be used as part of the enemy's standalone repertoire of attacks. For instance, the Samurai General can attack with a perilous Circular Sword Sweep completely unprompted by any of your actions, but deflecting his slashes can also cause him to respond with this perilous attack. Knowing that this a possibility can help you anticipate the sweep and avoid being taken by surprise if he chooses to respond in this manner. Some enemies have a very limited set of reactions (or even none), while others (notably some of the sub-bosses and bosses) can have an intricate set of responses based on how you interact with them during Swordplay.

Certain attacks used in response can be very dangerous but may also offer an opportunity to create an opening if anticipated. As an example, if a specific opponent often responds with a predictable thrust attack after being forced to deflect, incorporate this into your strategy by purposefully causing it to deflect so you can counter its reactionary thrust with a Mikiri and severely weaken its Posture.

# > Swordplay Advice

How you approach Swordplay varies depending on the enemy. Some will require unrelenting aggression, so that you can trigger desirable responses. Others require a stalwart defense, usually to avoid certain responses, but most lie somewhere between the two, informed by a thorough understanding of the enemy's move-set and tendencies. Although the specifics of your Swordplay strategy need to cater to the opponent at hand, there are some fundamental skills and good habits that underpin any encounter:

1. Confirm all of your attacks: As mentioned in the Basic Attack section, keep your offense compact and don't unnecessarily overextend yourself. Try to visually confirm how your attacks are being dealt with by the enemy. If they are being guarded, then continue to attack and press your advantage. In the meantime, look out for a deflect - both the visual and audio cue are very apparent. If your attack is deflected, stop immediately and go on the defensive.  
2. Bait enemies into set responses: Think of your katana as a sort of probe you can use to manipulate the enemy and keep them under your control. Enemies tend to respond predictably after either guarding or deflecting an attack. Observe what these responses are and take a mental note of them so that you can fully take advantage next time.

# Perilous Attacks

Perilous Attacks are unguardable attacks designed to prevent you from simply relying on guarding and deflecting. They serve to add an extra layer of tension and complexity to battles. At certain times when engaging the enemy, the Japanese character for "danger" will flash on the screen. This Danger Symbol lets you know that the next attack from the enemy will be a Perilous Attack, and can't be guarded. The Loaded Umbrella can guard against certain Perilous Attacks, though.

Your reward for dealing with the incoming Perilous Attack correctly is handsome. Against many regular enemies it will allow you to perform a Deathblow instantly, and against bosses or tougher enemies it will result in heavy Posture damage, and very often an opportunity to land some hits to further deplete their Vitality and Posture. Once you become familiar with an enemy's patterns, a Perilous Attack goes from something to be feared, to an opportunity you look forward to.

![](images/567877dface5540760992e9268aa0018716d1aaadace3bd6e765cbd9d6f89f40.jpg)  
If you see the Danger Symbol against a spear-wielding enemy...

![](images/3ef79e1b084a1e55013210958f09b841ff4ee38eb42ddae53bfac50dd714b67b.jpg)  
Swordplay can be a beautiful thing.

3. Play with Intentionality: Whether you are attacking, guarding or deflecting, always commit to the action with a set purpose and goal in mind. While it can be tempting to continually press the attack button when on the offensive, or repeatedly press the guard button in the hopes of deflecting when on the defensive, try to avoid doing so. Not only will your results vastly improve, it will also make the game much more fulfilling and entertaining.

When the enemy unleashes a Perilous Attack, you must watch carefully to determine which of three possible attack types it is, and then react with the appropriate counter. These are the three types and your options for dealing with them:

# >Thrust

Thrust attacks can still be deflected, but the best way to deal with most of them is with a Mikiri Counter, by pressing the dodge button to dash into it. Doing so will result in three times as much Posture damage as from a deflect, and the timing is much more lenient. This only works if you've unlocked the Mikiri Skill, however. Mikiri is one of the first Skills you can learn from the Shinobi Arts skill-tree. Overall the risk-reward ratio is far more in your favor by trying to Mikiri Counter a Perilous Attack thrust compared to deflecting it. However, against strings with multiple stabbing thrust attacks, the highest reward is gained by deflecting the first couple of hits, and then using Mikiri on the final one.

![](images/74473ddd2e007d210fe20e14d22758a1373613a788b5c5e907fc1ccd2632ccf4.jpg)  
...there's a good chance a Mikiri Counter will be the correct response.

![](images/03e4994f154dc57290a8fcb31dc1fe3572c2baf8399d27af641ea44027cd6d14.jpg)  
Learn to recognize thrust animations so you can use a Mikiri Counter in time.

# > Sweep

Sweep attacks are always considered Perilous Attacks and need to be avoided with a jump. Make sure the jump is a neutral jump, and that you're not pressing any direction on the analogue stick; if you jump away from the enemy you'll still avoid the sweep, but you won't be able to punish them. Once directly above the enemy, press

A/ to perform a Jump-Kick Counter, again resulting in heavy Posture damage and often further aerial hits. You can also transition into mid-air Combat Arts or Prosthetic Tools (if you have the skills unlocked) after a Jump-Kick Counter.

![](images/171712789ae5741ddf5d4a7ce91bc4bd1fa1f8d06f193afa296236ff430ae429.jpg)  
The moment you jump you will be invulnerable to all sweep attacks, so even if you see the attack touch your legs, you will still be safe. Avoiding sweeps by dodging is not possible.

# >Grab

Using a step dodge is generally the most effective way of dealing with grabs. While less evasive than a jump, a dodge recovers much faster, allowing you to attack the enemy after their grab attempt. Be sure to time your step dodge well, just before the grab connects. If you step dodge too early many grabs will re-orient and catch you.

![](images/35cd0dc9d6f002b1d23f8f24dd5a3cb731f8f15bd74d795765588cb49091e914.jpg)  
Step dodging away from a grab allows you to stay close enough to punish their recovery.

A step dodge can more specifically be separated into dodge left, dodge right and a backward dodge. Certain Perilous Attacks can only be stepped in one direction. Grabs often have a wide horizontal reach, so you'll need to backstep, however a lunging grab will generally require you to step laterally. There are also sweeping grabs and thrusting grabs. Sweeping grabs are best avoided by jumping over them, and can't be guarded by the Loaded Umbrella. A good example of this is the Chained Ogre's lunging grab. Thrusting grabs can be deflected, but the safest option is to dodge sideways to avoid them. A good example of an enemy who uses thrusting grabs are the Snake Eyes sub-bosses.

# Jumping Away

Of course, jumping away from the enemy is another option when you see a Perilous Attack coming. If you're not familiar with the enemy's moveset and are not sure what the attack is, quickly create space between you and the opponent with a backward jump. Most, but not all, Perilous Attacks will miss, though you generally won't be able to punish the enemy while they recover, especially against bosses.

The following table summarizes all the ways of dealing with Perilous Attacks:

<table><tr><td></td><td>Thrust</td><td>Sweep</td><td>Grab</td></tr><tr><td>Deflect</td><td>-</td><td>×</td><td>×</td></tr><tr><td>Mikiri</td><td>○</td><td>×</td><td>×</td></tr><tr><td>Jump</td><td>×</td><td>○</td><td>-</td></tr><tr><td>Dodge</td><td>-*</td><td>×</td><td>○</td></tr></table>

*sideways only  
Recommended X Will Take Damage -Possible but not recommended

# >Lightning Reversal

One final Perilous Attack that requires a very specific reaction is a Lightning Reversal. Against these you can jump and absorb the lighting into your katana, and then press  $\mathbb{R}\mathbb{B} / \mathbb{R}\mathbb{I}$  to unleash it before you hit the ground to discharge it. If this hits an enemy, it will inflict massive Vitality and Posture damage through a Lightning Reversal. Such attacks are very rare, though, and will be pointed out specifically in the enemy strategy sections of the Opposing Forces chapter. You can also check the Status Abnormality section on Shock for more information (P.38).

![](images/d9cc050f1f904bfb42a0e2750c8ffaecbf766236b206772558239dfffb265f68.jpg)  
This Perilous Attack is an opportunity for a Lightning Reversal.

# Baiting and Punishing

In many action games, baiting the enemy to attack by staying at their maximum range, and then avoiding their attack at the last moment so you can punish them while they recover, is a very common, even ubiquitous, tactic. While baiting and punishing is still useful in Sekiro, it is merely a situational tactic—one of many within a complex myriad of options that includes guarding, step dodging, deflecting as well as prudent use of Prosthetic Tools and Combat Arts. This is not to say that baiting and punishing is not useful—far from it; it is still an effective strategy, particularly against larger enemies with slower wind-up and attacks that recover slowly, such as the Chained Ogre.

Just know that many attacks, especially those of bosses, begin and recover far too quickly to make baiting and punishing a viable or consistent strategy against them. While your step dodge and jump also have a limited period of invulnerability at the start, most attacks track too well to really take advantage of this. Instead you are encouraged to close the gap and engage the enemy in the multilayered Swordplay system. This is best exemplified in the control system; pressing the step dodge button won't perform an evasive backstep, but instead makes you dash forwards.

# Hit Reactions

# > Posture-broken

Having your Posture depleted doesn't mean that enemies can land a Deathblow on you; you will, however, be placed in a Posture-broken state that leaves you immobile and vulnerable to further damage. While in the Posture-broken state, after a brief period of immobility you will be able to safety roll in any direction by pressing the left analogue stick in conjunction with the A/ or B/ buttons.

If you ever find yourself knocked to the ground by an enemy attack you can also perform a safety roll. This will usually be your best option for getting back up to your feet. Many enemies have attacks that will hit you while you're on the floor, but thankfully the safety roll has a significant amount of invulnerability, so if you time it right, you can avoid incoming attacks and get up safely. This is especially evident when dealing with enemy sweep attacks. A normal standing step dodge does not have enough invulnerability to evade a sweep attack, but if the enemy is trying to hit you with one while you're on the ground, a safety roll will avoid it.

![](images/67a1ecc7d1b01a2127f532cab8526df399546f8606870e5b5975b466bafe8518.jpg)  
Safety roll has a long period of invulnerability during the beginning of its animation, allowing you to slip away from incoming danger.

![](images/95be095b33b05cd7d12312223042cd8ff31a94e4f2e34b8ce0f9ae88091d70b1.jpg)  
Punishing enemy attacks requires patience and timing.

Along with the Posture-broken state there are a wide variety of other hit reaction types. Here are some of the most important:

# > Flinching

This is the most frequent type of hit reaction you'll encounter. It doesn't last very long but interrupts your actions and momentarily prevents you from attacking. The available recovery options from a flinch are guard, deflect, or step dodge.

# > Stumble

A stumble will cause you to lose your balance and take a few steps before falling to the ground. This leaves you vulnerable to further attacks, but doesn't last as long as a proper knockdown. One of the unique recovery options you can adopt from a stumble is a Brace Guard, which effectively operates like a standard guard. Available recovery options from a stumble are: attack, Brace Guard (before falling) and a safety roll (when on the ground)

# > Knockdown

Being knocked down will cause you to fall flat on the ground, where you are completely defenseless against enemy attacks. This state lasts a few seconds until you slowly push yourself back up to your feet. This is most commonly caused by powerful vertical attacks that hit with enough force to flatten you, but a knockdown can also occur when damage is taken after being Posture-broken. Also, most grab attacks feature unique animations but ultimately leave you in a knockdown state. As with a Posture-break, the only available recovery option after a knockdown is a Safety Roll.

Some powerful rising blows or grabs can launch you upwards before hitting the ground and entering a Knockdown state. It's generally impossible to perform any recovery actions while in mid-air so this takes you out of the battle for at least a few seconds. However, if you see a Grapple Point while flying you can latch onto it. This is extremely situational, however, and is only an option against a few opponents.

# Enemy Stun

While most weaker enemies are briefly stunned after being hit by an attack, allowing you to attempt a follow-up attack, some enemies will resist these stuns and power through your attack; they receive Vitality and Posture damage, but otherwise appear to ignore it. There are two distinct systems that handle how and why an enemy will resist the stun from your attacks: Super Armor and Armored Attacks.

Which system is in play for any given enemy is dependent on whether that enemy engages in Swordplay. The only thing you need to know about Swordplay is whether the enemy is capable of guarding and deflecting. Simply put—with very few exceptions—if an enemy cannot guard or deflect, they do not engage in Swordplay, whereas enemies that can guard do engage in Swordplay.

# >Super Armor

Non-Swordplay enemies (those who cannot guard) cannot be stunned by your attacks until a certain condition is met. This condition is governed by a hidden "super armor" gauge that starts at a set value for each enemy and depletes with every attack until it reaches zero. Each of the different damaging attacks available to you has a corresponding super armor damage value that depletes that gauge. Once the gauge reaches zero, the enemy's super armor is broken and the attack that reduces it to zero will stun them for a brief duration, allowing you to deal extra damage until they recover. The type and duration of this stun is dependent upon the enemy—some are stunned for several seconds, others only briefly. They won't receive any further super armor damage during this stun, and their super armor gauge will completely refresh to full once the stun is over. In addition, failing to deal any Vitality damage to a super armored enemy for a set duration will also cause their super armor gauge to refresh to full. Fortunately, this timer resets every time they take damage.

Let's look at the Chained Ogre in Ashina Outskirts as an example of this super armor system in action. The Chained Ogre has a super armor gauge value of 400, and his gauge refreshes seven seconds after damage is received.

<table><tr><td colspan="2">Super Armor Damage</td></tr><tr><td>Normal Attack</td><td>40</td></tr><tr><td>Thrust</td><td>80</td></tr><tr><td>Mid-Air Attack</td><td>20 x2</td></tr><tr><td>Counter-Slash</td><td>40</td></tr><tr><td>Dodge Counterattack</td><td>40</td></tr><tr><td>Sprinting Attack</td><td>40</td></tr></table>

If your basic attack deals 40 super armor damage, then you won't spun the Chained Ogre until you've landed at least 10 attacks. Since he's very aggressive, you have virtually no chance to land that many attacks without using hit-and-run tactics to avoid his attacks and punish him as he recovers. His super armor gauge will recover back to the full 400 within seven seconds of taking no damage, so you can't be too passive. You must actively move closer to him to provoke him to use attacks that you can avoid and punish with the seven second window, or you'll lose all your progress towards stunning him. Successfully managing to accomplish this is rewarded with a stun that allows you to deal several more blows to him.

![](images/6ca03330500e752385a0fe9845f6306e0e53ce7973928a52d6cdd70021e021da.jpg)  
The Chained Ogre in Ashina Outskirts is the quintessential Super Armor enemy.

A small wrinkle in this system is that some very strong super armor enemies also use powerful attacks that will ignore incoming super armor damage. Even if their current super armor gauge is currently at, for the sake of example, a lowly 10, meaning any attack that hits them should stun, they will ignore any incoming super armor damage during their attack and therefore cannot be stunned. The Chained Ogre has an attack that serves as an example of this: if you attempt to attack him during his powerful Dropkick attack you will deal no super armor damage to him—even while he is recovering! This means it is impossible to break his super armor during this attack.

For this reason, when fighting enemies with super armor it's best not to challenge their attacks directly, even if you believe your next hit will stun them, otherwise you run the risk of taking a damaging blow. You'll find a full list of enemies with super armor at the start of the Opposing Forces chapter (P.344). More details relating to enemies that use super armor are to be found in the attack tables for each enemy in that chapter.

# > Armored Attacks

Most enemies that engage in swordplay do not use the super armor system. Instead, they have individual armored attacks that resist stuns only for the duration of that specific attack. The entire attack isn't always armored; sometimes only the wind-up will be,

# Enemy Types

To make breaking down enemies a more logical process, we've split them into four main categories: Normal, Strong, Sub-Boss and Boss. The Opposing Forces chapter of this book follows that order, and most enemies fall very obviously into one of these categories.

Certain enemy types in Sekiro have specific weaknesses that you can take advantage of, simply because they are of a particular type. This is unrelated to their category, and has a more direct impact on fighting them. One or more of these types can apply to an enemy, but the majority of enemies are subject to none of them. We'll go through each of the possible types here.

# Blinding Enemies

Note that the blinding pun applied by the Shinobi Firecracker Prosthetic Tool and Fistful of Ash item is independent of the pun from breaking super armor. Unfortunately, both methods of blinding enemies share a cooldown when used against super armored enemies. As an example, the Chained Ogre has a 15 second cool down, and this means you can only temporarily blind him with either Ash or Firecrackers once every 15 seconds. Using either of these methods will set off the cooldown of the other, so it isn't possible to alternate between Ash and Firecrackers to blind these enemies twice in a row.

and sometimes only part of a combo has a single armored attack within it. The only time these enemies can resist stuns is during the armored portions of these attacks. At any other time they can be stunned by hitting their body or interrupted by forcing them to guard.

The stun resistance of an armored attack is not reliant on a gauge or timer, and your attacks' super armor values are only a rough guide to how well they will fare against an armored attack. Armored attacks are capable of resisting stuns in a binary fashion; either the attack you are using will break their armor and stun them, or it will not. Certain strong attacks, such as Ichimonji or the Loaded Axe, are generally good at breaking through armored attacks and stunning the enemy, but whether your attacks can stun any given armored attack is determined on a case-by-case basis. Most armored attacks will easily power through light attacks such as your basic attacks, counter-slashes, or the Loaded Shuriken, while some armored attacks cannot be broken at all.

As a general rule of thumb, many slow, powerful techniques such as Perilous Attacks, tend to be armored attacks, but you'll also often find this kind of armor on escape moves such as dashes, or attacks with strong momentum such as leaping attacks. Armored attacks are indicated in the respective enemy attack tables in the Opposing Forces Chapter.

The time of day changes over the course of the game, progressing from Morning to Night. You'll see these icons used throughout this book whenever something is specific to a time of day:

They boast enhanced stats, such as attack power, Vitality and Posture. These enemies start appearing at various spots in areas you've already explored. # Status Effects

In Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice there are both Status Abnormalities and Status Buffs. The former can be used to cripple your enemies; be careful, however, as you are susceptible to them too. Status Buffs can give you a massive advantage in battle when used wisely.

# Status Abnormalities

There are five status abnormalities that can be inflicted: Burn, Poison, Terror, Shock and Enfeeblement. They all result in dangerous and potentially lethal effects. Of these status abnormalities, you can also inflict three of them upon enemies: Burn, Poison and Shock. Terror and Enfeeblement can only be inflicted upon you.

How close you are to being afflicted with a status abnormality is represented by a gauge in the middle of the screen. Once you are under the effect of a Status Abnormality, it will be indicated by an icon underneath your Vitality gauge If you're attempting to inflict an abnormality on an enemy, however, there is no gauge showing the build-up of the status.

>Burn  

<table><tr><td>炎</td></tr></table>

<table><tr><td>Damage</td><td>1% Vitality per second</td></tr><tr><td>Duration</td><td>10 seconds</td></tr><tr><td>Total Damage</td><td>10% of Vitality</td></tr><tr><td>Other Effects</td><td>Halts Posture recovery</td></tr></table>

Burn is inflicted when you or the enemy take a certain amount of Fire-based damage. The amount of burn build-up can be sharply increased by first dousing an enemy in oil.

![](images/8acb3dd530aafbef70fa3e48e6e64656f536ee0082b366f0d70fc48062042b81.jpg)  
An enemy doused in oil will is set alight much more easily.

Upon being afflicted with Burn, an enemy will enter an agonized stun state. How long this lasts depends on the enemy in question; you yourself will not enter this stun state upon being burnt.

![](images/ed2779aeb35964aa963c276a3d1a412ecbca4a8b7e7255ff99fe83e9acaf73e6.jpg)  
Touching fire in the environment will cause the Burn status to build up.

Fire damage, along with the Burn status abnormality, is very effective Red-Eyed enemies, since they innately fear Fire. At the mere sight of Fire, they will go into a panic frenzy for about five seconds. This gives you ample time to continue dealing Fire-based damage or land a couple of attacks. A red-eyed enemy can be panic stunned up to three times before it stops having any effect. There's also a cooldown on this panic, so you can't just repeatedly panic them. After the enemy has been Burnt, this counter will reset. Do watch out, though; the enemy will be immune to the panic frenzy during certain attacks, so be sure to use your Fire attack while they are recovering from a previous attack. Another point to note is that inflicting Burn on Undead Prisoners will prevent them from coming back to life.

![](images/1a60379d3514bdd944e7085a784f14daca1ed23e62aaa5be28e84c201bac3c5e.jpg)  
The Chained Ogre in Ashina Outskirts fears Fire.

# > Poisson

![](images/69606ee79ae785dd63448c4776be7b8e1134ccc32fd885da942b0e3da334cac8.jpg)

Poison is a dangerous status abnormality that lasts for 40 seconds. Depending on the size of your Vitality gauge, it can deplete anywhere from 30 to  $80\%$  of your Vitality in that time, but on your first playthrough it's going to be closer to the latter.

As mentioned in the Enemy Types section, Blue-Rust Poison from the Sabimaru is incredibly effective against Okami enemies. Not only does it lead to massive Posture damage when they are inflicted with Poison, it also leads to a unique vomit stun that allows you to land multiple hits. There are three ways of treating and preventing Poison, one of which is very indirect.

The Green Mossy Twisted Gourd and Antidote Powder are very much analogous to the Red Gourd and Ministry Dousing Powder. Again, the Green Gourd has no effect if you are already poisoned; it is a preventative item.

The final method to counteract enemy Poison is by poisoning yourself! Contact Medicine inflicts you with a weaker poison that drains less than a third of the health of regular enemy Poison, and also lasts 40 seconds. While poisoned by Contact Medicine, you cannot be poisoned by regular Poison.

Another purpose for Contact Medicine is that while poisoned you can use the Mist Raven technique without needing to be hit by an enemy attack first. You can use this to quickly and safely teleport through difficulty areas (at the cost of two Spirit Emblems per Mist Warp) or with the Great Feather Mist Raven, turn the battlefield into a raging inferno for a short period of time.

# > Terror

![](images/495503feb24d5e6ab7967f48186a2bc302d2c725b626418aab3b1532e93e0e16.jpg)

Terror is a lethal status ailment that instantly kills you once the gauge is full. You are quite literally scared to death. Fortunately, only a handful of enemies in the game inflict this status. Terror gauge build-up can be removed by the Mottled Purple Twisted Gourd, which

works in a similar way to the Red or Green Gourd, in that it removes any existing Terror build-up as well providing resistance for 30 seconds. Pacifying Agents are analogous to Antidote Powder or Ministry Dousing Powder. As well as removing active Terror gauge build-up, they provide extra resistance against Terror build-up for 30 seconds. However, neither has any effect if you are already terrified, because you are dead.

# >Shock

![](images/95439e185e603344081f72a9b0756fb0ffbb0b45274a6ec2b0d02a6b24d1875b.jpg)

If your feet are on the ground as you get hit by a lightning attack, you will take a large amount of Vitality and Posture damage. The amount varies depending on your Vitality.

As well as taking damage, you will also enter a three second stun that leaves you completely vulnerable to attack. However, by jumping into the air as the lightning hits you, it will transfer to your katana instead. While you'll still take minimal damage, you won't go into shock. After a brief aerial stun, you can then discharge the lightning by pressing RB/RI. This will result in a spectacular display called a Lightning Reversal which will inflict shock on the enemy instead, resulting in major damage and a temporary stun. Be sure to quickly discharge the lightning while in the air, because as soon as your feet hit the ground you will go into shock.

![](images/00605fd4b5ce3bbc8ecab48154590d7078fc783f472193bf8daf7a8088b28c44.jpg)  
Shock stuns you for three seconds and deals severe Vitality damage.

![](images/72801de083de7a6bff7b5930f8edda3b6dae9275f5bf0af1ab851a0ba3de879a.jpg)

# Enfeeblement

![](images/f0a0bdaf330a907bc6489ead2dd1da9db13e265c6a0807b7a94f3fdfed3ad62d.jpg)

Enfeeblement is a very unique status ailment. It is only inflicted by a single enemy, late in the game. When this enemy plays its flute it will increase the status gauge, draining your youth. Once the bar is full you will be

![](images/5b9d25fb8ec8ff15ef45d5e105bcd671911eea3a2ab927d0a451e0bb388e0603.jpg)

You can take your youth back if if you manage to kill one of the enemies that can cause the Status Abnormality.

left old and infirm. In this state you are practically useless; left with only a sliver of health, a pathetic, stumbling attack, and unable to use any prosthetics or items. Also, if you die in this state then you cannot resurrect.

There are three ways to gain your youth back. Either stay alive for 30 seconds, and the Enfeebled ailment will naturally reverse. Or, if you manage to kill enemy (it doesn't necessarily need to be the one who took your youth) then you will, quite literally, suck your youth back. We recommend you try to see this animation at least once because it is as disgusting as it is satisfying. Finally, you can remove the ailment by reaching a Sculptor's Idol and resting.

# Upgrades

As you progress through the game you'll be able to upgrade your Vitality, Posture, Attack Power, Healing Gourd as well as learn new Skills and develop new Prosthetic Tools. The challenges you face will progressively escalate, so it's imperative that you continually upgrade your abilities to match, to avoid being underpowered against the tougher foes to come.

![](images/d0c718774d7fbd09b53df9ce5a23cef1d8d2ede19d30628ec095505d683e1fc6.jpg)

# Vitality & Prayer Beads

Prayer Beads are generally acquired after defeating sub-bosses, but some are also bought from vendors or found hidden in the environment. If you collect four, head to the Sculptor's Idol Menu, select Enhance Physical Attributes, and then convert them into a Prayer Necklace, which will enhance your Vitality and Posture. With each necklace your Vitality and Posture will increase by a set amount;  $25\%$  of their base value. You start with 10 Vitality, and can gain 10 Prayer Necklaces to increase your Vitality to a maximum of 20. At this point you'll have over three times as much Vitality and Posture as when you first started the game. Unlike with Attack Power, however, you can never go above that amount, even on New Game+.

![](images/bda473a1fbce22a534900446a85f2e9e0bffc3a15750c8121d06fb1f5238b3c7.jpg)

# Attack Power & Memories

Raising your Attack Power is the only way to increase your raw offensive capabilities. This statistic influences the damage dealt by all your offensive options, including katana slashes, Prosthetic Tools, Combat Arts, and even the amount of Posture damage inflicted to your opponents after deflecting their strikes. As such, raising your Attack Power can have a dramatic impact on your success throughout the game. Every time you defeat a boss, you'll receive a Memory of that battle. By selecting the Enhance Attack Power option in the Sculptor's Idol Menu, you can increase your current Attack Power by 1. This should always be done immediately after defeating a boss. Once the Memory has been used, it will be stored in your inventory as a Remnant. These items provide interesting background lore on vanquished foes, so be sure to inspect them.

The first 13 Attack Power upgrades will increase the strength of all your attacks by the same amount for each point gained. At this stage, raising your Attack Power by a few more points can make an incredible difference in your damage output, so going out of your way to defeat optional bosses is well worth the effort. 14 is the maximum you can obtain from defeating all bosses in a single playthrough, but it's possible to raise your Attack Power to a total of 99 by defeating the bosses and obtaining their Memories again on multiple New Game+ cycles, or through the Dancing Dragon Mask. The returns for each new point of Attack Power gained diminish sharply after your first playthrough, but continuing to raise this statistic still makes a significant difference and is essential to beating the higher difficulty levels.

# Dancing Dragon Mask

By acquiring all three Mask Fragments—Right, Left and Dragon—you will restore the Dancing Dragon Mask. Once you have the complete mask you'll gain a new option at Sculptor's Idols, letting you convert Skill Points into attack power at a rate of five Skill Points for one point of Attack Power. The mask presents you with an interesting dilemma: do you spend your Skill Points acquiring more skills, opening up new combat options, or do you use them to increase your Attack Power and increase the potency of what you already have.

Until you've actually purchased and experimented with many of the skills, it would be hard to gauge whether or not they fit your play style. Heavy investment into Attack Power through the Dancing Dragon Mask is something that you'll generally do once your knowledge of the game is quite high and you're looking to maximize the efficiency of a new playthrough. If you're having trouble against a particular boss, however, gaining a couple of extra Attack Power rather than a new skill can often give you just enough of an edge to attain victory.

# Skill Points

By defeating enemies and bosses you will gain Skill EXP, as indicated by the Skill EXP Gauge to the top right of the HUD (or at the bottom right when the game is paused). When enough Skill EXP is acquired and the gauge is filled, you'll gain one Skill Point. Skill Points can be spent by sitting at a Sculptor's Idol and choosing Learn Skill. You must first have an Esoteric Text in your possession so that a skill tree is available. It will take 125 Skill Points to unlock all skills, not to mention any that you might want to invest into Attack Power with the Dancing Dragon Mask, so you're going to need a lot of them. Check P.539 for a breakdown of the areas that provide the most Skill EXP if you're looking to maximize your gains. See table opposite for the Skill EXP required to unlock each Skill Point.

![](images/c187a610966864c8ff119d5730cfa1f405e8db57fff36368d220c9d15890af7e.jpg)

# Gourd Seeds

![](images/94bee1ca1ee18f75d17f9126da129b7655bf0842e5655b10c3a420064a40a337.jpg)  
Sub-bosses tend to give a lot of Skill EXP upon defeat.

Dotted around the Ashina lands you'll occasionally find Gourd Seeds. By talking to Emma and then selecting Give Gourd Seed you can enhance your Healing Gourd. With each Gourd Seed that you find and give her, the number of Healing Gourd uses increases by one. You can find nine Gourd Seeds, for a maximum of ten Healing Gourd uses. The Healing Gourd cannot be enhanced any further beyond that.

![](images/8cfafe64d8a87ea5843abdda5f6c21ab83b36abcbc7afdf0b7c1463ce958f22e.jpg)  
Ashina Outskirts Kill General Naomi Kawarada.

![](images/2e3d22a8143612563e01219718aa5c1714ca4b011c2f36c6b5fcde18cee60bb1.jpg)  
Ashina Outskirts Buy from the Battlefield Memorial Mob for 1000 Sen.

![](images/7a6536796f65abfd5935788d2e6eddd141562c9d0dc01fb0c2573cc87c517e26.jpg)  
Ashina Outskirts Just after the Chained Ogre near the Outskirts Wall - Stairway idol. Grapple onto the hole in the wall and turn left.

![](images/5e59bff8ae1ff6f96a950e7b4e245f7481ff717b0e7d6eb7aefa47a125ea7b8c.jpg)  
Ashina Outskirts Fujioka the Info Broker will open up shop in the Dilapidated Temple if you defeat the nearby samurai for him in Ashina Castle, or defeat Genichiro Ashina. He sells one for 2000 Sen.

![](images/f8388dc04320b48c76fe1fc59ff3234c7f7687e1971953edfd84769d2ffe7279.jpg)  
Ashina Castle Just before the Antechamber Idol there's one in a Treasure Chest.

![](images/05a40736e47234bf8b6559ec1dd655a0d31c5ef3dffd81563e9bce157b714a65.jpg)  
Senpou Temple Near the beginning, inside a temple where three Seekers and an Infested Seeker are praying.

![](images/be6f290cb234506d4216883ed9af6780834e61c6aec58e039e5c91f554382276.jpg)  
Sunken Valley From the Under-Shrine Valley. Idol, head north and you'll soon see a grapple point guarded by a Valley Clan member on the cliffside to your right; make your way there and keep going up until you reach a hut. The seed is in the corner next to it.

![](images/e78bdb917ace9588d4be9b5331ceb2a27e72ab3b14a6f0ecda85dc436ac26036.jpg)  
Ashina Depths In Mibu Village at the base of a massive illuminated cherry. It's surrounded by Mibu Villagers that try to grab you, so be careful.

![](images/ac0d69482ef5944b2529064a94e218690b9a1e444fae8ea0eaff64a9b9986f52.jpg)  
Fountainhead Palace Just after the Palace Grounds Idol in a chest surrounded by Red-robed Palace Nobles.

# Difficulty Modifiers

As you progress through the land of Ashina, your enemies will become more and more formidable. With each successive journey, the challenge will rise to meet your ever-developing skills. For the bravest of players, there are several options to make the struggles that you face even more daunting...

# Time of Day

Morning

Noon

Evening

Night

Bell Demon

Defeating certain key bosses as you play through the game will not only advance the story, but it will also advance the time of day the game takes place in. Along with a visual change to areas, enemies will become increasingly more difficult as the time of day progresses. When you awake in the Dilapidated Temple it will be Morning, and then after defeating either Genichiro Ashina in Ashina Castle, or Corrupted Monk (Illusion) in Ashina Depths, the time of day will advance to Noon. To advance time again to Evening you'll

need to defeat three out of the four key bosses available to you at this stage. In addition to the two already mentioned, the other ones are: Folding Screen Monkeys in Senpou Temple, Mt. Kongo and Guardian Ape in Sunken Valley Passage. After entering Fountainhead Palace, it will then shift to Night. The values here show the extent to which enemies get more powerful during each time of day.

After you beat the game, you are given an option to start a second playthrough. If you select No, then you can continue to stay in the current playthrough until you decide to move on by accessing the Sculptor's Idol in the Dilapidated Temple and picking Start Playthrough #2. On your second run, the enemies will be even more ferocious than before, but the amount of Sen and Skill Points that you gain also increases proportionately.

# New Game++ and Beyond

You can continue to play New Game+ multiple times through, and with each playthrough the strength of the enemies, and amount of rewards, will get increasingly greater. On top of all the normal modifier increases, once you reach New Game++, the Super Armor Damage you deal is reduced by the values given in the table below, making it much harder to break enemy super armor with each subsequent playthrough. Against enemies that have Super Armor this can have a huge impact on their difficulty. The difficulty increases will cap out on your 8th playthrough, so from the 9th onwards everything will be at the same difficulty.

![](images/7d9e309ec8d9e8581d14a41a8964cb0905ffd7931f50258d3b84dc45ff1929c9.jpg)  
The option for "Start Playthrough #2" can only be found at the Sculptor's Idol in the Dilapidated Temple area.

*These values only impact player attacks.

Upon beating the game and seeing any of the endings, you'll receive an item called Kuro's Charm. Give this to Lord Kuro during the Prologue, and you will activate Hard Mode. This is represented by the Japanese character for "difficult" under your Vitality gauge. It will also be shown next to your save file.

Hard mode greatly increases the amount of Vitality and Posture that enemies have. Aside from making them more powerful, it also makes them deal  $30\%$  Vitality damage even on guard, so deflecting becomes much more important. Note that there is no way to

mitigate this extra damage unless you deflect, not even the Loaded Umbrella can prevent it. As a small consolation you also receive  $20\%$  more Sen and Skill Points. These effects stack on top of those of New Game+, and to make matters worse, enemies on Hard Mode New Game+ also gain some additional Poison resistance.

You can back out of Hard Mode at any time by talking to the Sculptor and picking "Avoid additional hardships". If you take back Kuro's Charm, you cannot go back to Hard Mode until the next playthrough.

# New Game+ on Hard Mode

If you're looking for the most extreme levels of difficulty, then you're going to want to start a New Game+ cycle as soon as possible and give Lord Kuro back his charm to activate Hard Mode. The stat increases that enemies receive from activating Hard Mode on New Game+ are significantly bigger than those on New Game, putting an even greater emphasis on being intimately familiar with their attack patterns. This is also the fastest way to earn Sen and Skill EXP, as you can see from the values in the table here.
